## Solution

**Setup.** Place the cone with apex at the origin and axis along the $z$-axis. The base is the disk $x^2+y^2\le R^2$ at $z=h$, and the cone surface is $x^2+y^2\le (Rz/h)^2$, $0\le z\le h$. The total volume is $V=\tfrac13\pi R^2 h$.

**The cutting plane.** The plane is tangent to the base circle $x^2+y^2=R^2$ (at $z=h)$. The tangent point is $(R,0,h)$, so the plane contains the tangent line $\{x=R,\, z=h\}$. The plane also passes through the midpoint of the altitude, $(0,0,h/2)$. A plane containing $\{x=R,\,z=h\}$ has the form $a(x-R)+b(z-h)=0$. Substituting $(0,0,h/2)$:

$$a(0-R)+b(h/2-h)=0 \implies -aR - bh/2=0 \implies a=-bh/(2R).$$

This gives the plane $z = \tfrac{h}{2}\!\left(1+\tfrac{x}{R}\right)$.

**Identifying the smaller part.** At $z=0$ the plane gives $x=-R$ (entire apex disk is below); at $z=h$ it gives $x=R$ (tangent, entire base is above). The region **below** the plane (containing the apex) is the smaller part.

**Volume below the plane.** A point $(x,y,z)$ in the cone below the plane satisfies
$$\frac{h}{R}\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\;\le\; z \;\le\; \frac{h}{2}\!\left(1+\frac{x}{R}\right).$$
This requires $\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\le \tfrac{R+x}{2}$, i.e. the shadow in the $xy$-plane. The volume is

$$V_{\text{below}}=\frac{h}{R}\iint_{\text{shadow}}\left[\frac{R+x}{2}-\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\right]dx\,dy.$$

**Polar coordinates.** Set $x=\rho\cos\theta$, $y=\rho\sin\theta$. The shadow becomes $\rho\le R/(2-\cos\theta)$. Writing $b=2-\cos\theta$ and $\rho_{\max}=R/b$:

$$\int_0^{R/b}\!\left[\frac{R+\rho\cos\theta}{2}-\rho\right]\rho\,d\rho = \int_0^{R/b}\!\left[\frac{R\rho}{2}-\frac{b\rho^2}{2}\right]d\rho = \frac{R^3}{12\,b^2}.$$

Therefore

$$V_{\text{below}}=\frac{h}{R}\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{R^3}{12(2-\cos\theta)^2}\,d\theta = \frac{hR^2}{12}\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{d\theta}{(2-\cos\theta)^2}.$$

**Evaluating the integral.** Using the standard result (obtained by differentiating $\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{d\theta}{a-\cos\theta}=\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{a^2-1}}$ with respect to $a$):

$$\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{d\theta}{(a-\cos\theta)^2}=\frac{2\pi a}{(a^2-1)^{3/2}},\qquad a>1.$$

With $a=2$:

$$\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{d\theta}{(2-\cos\theta)^2}=\frac{4\pi}{3\sqrt{3}}.$$

**Final computation.**

$$V_{\text{below}}=\frac{hR^2}{12}\cdot\frac{4\pi}{3\sqrt{3}}=\frac{\pi R^2 h}{9\sqrt{3}}.$$

Since $V=\tfrac13\pi R^2 h$:

$$\frac{V_{\text{below}}}{V}=\frac{\pi R^2 h/(9\sqrt3)}{\pi R^2 h/3}=\frac{1}{3\sqrt3}=\frac{\sqrt3}{9}\approx 0.192<\frac12.$$

So the below part is indeed the smaller part.

$$\boxed{V_{\text{smaller}}=\dfrac{V}{3\sqrt{3}}=\dfrac{V\sqrt{3}}{9}}$$

### PROOF COMPLETE

## Solution

**Setup.** Place the cone with apex at the origin and axis along the $z$-axis. The base is the disk $x^2+y^2\le R^2$ at $z=h$, and the cone surface is $x^2+y^2\le (Rz/h)^2$, $0\le z\le h$. The total volume is $V=\tfrac13\pi R^2 h$.

**The cutting plane.** The plane is tangent to the base circle $x^2+y^2=R^2$ (at $z=h)$. The tangent point is $(R,0,h)$, so the plane contains the tangent line $\{x=R,\, z=h\}$. The plane also passes through the midpoint of the altitude, $(0,0,h/2)$. A plane containing $\{x=R,\,z=h\}$ has the form $a(x-R)+b(z-h)=0$. Substituting $(0,0,h/2)$:

$$a(0-R)+b(h/2-h)=0 \implies -aR - bh/2=0 \implies a=-bh/(2R).$$

This gives the plane $z = \tfrac{h}{2}\!\left(1+\tfrac{x}{R}\right)$.

**Identifying the smaller part.** At $z=0$ the plane gives $x=-R$ (entire apex disk is below); at $z=h$ it gives $x=R$ (tangent, entire base is above). The region **below** the plane (containing the apex) is the smaller part.

**Volume below the plane.** A point $(x,y,z)$ in the cone below the plane satisfies
$$\frac{h}{R}\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\;\le\; z \;\le\; \frac{h}{2}\!\left(1+\frac{x}{R}\right).$$
This requires $\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\le \tfrac{R+x}{2}$, i.e. the shadow in the $xy$-plane. The volume is

$$V_{\text{below}}=\frac{h}{R}\iint_{\text{shadow}}\left[\frac{R+x}{2}-\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\right]dx\,dy.$$

**Polar coordinates.** Set $x=\rho\cos\theta$, $y=\rho\sin\theta$. The shadow becomes $\rho\le R/(2-\cos\theta)$. Writing $b=2-\cos\theta$ and $\rho_{\max}=R/b$:

$$\int_0^{R/b}\!\left[\frac{R+\rho\cos\theta}{2}-\rho\right]\rho\,d\rho = \int_0^{R/b}\!\left[\frac{R\rho}{2}-\frac{b\rho^2}{2}\right]d\rho = \frac{R^3}{12\,b^2}.$$

Therefore

$$V_{\text{below}}=\frac{h}{R}\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{R^3}{12(2-\cos\theta)^2}\,d\theta = \frac{hR^2}{12}\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{d\theta}{(2-\cos\theta)^2}.$$

**Evaluating the integral.** Using the standard result (obtained by differentiating $\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{d\theta}{a-\cos\theta}=\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{a^2-1}}$ with respect to $a$):

$$\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{d\theta}{(a-\cos\theta)^2}=\frac{2\pi a}{(a^2-1)^{3/2}},\qquad a>1.$$

With $a=2$:

$$\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{d\theta}{(2-\cos\theta)^2}=\frac{4\pi}{3\sqrt{3}}.$$

**Final computation.**

$$V_{\text{below}}=\frac{hR^2}{12}\cdot\frac{4\pi}{3\sqrt{3}}=\frac{\pi R^2 h}{9\sqrt{3}}.$$

Since $V=\tfrac13\pi R^2 h$:

$$\frac{V_{\text{below}}}{V}=\frac{\pi R^2 h/(9\sqrt3)}{\pi R^2 h/3}=\frac{1}{3\sqrt3}=\frac{\sqrt3}{9}\approx 0.192<\frac12.$$

So the below part is indeed the smaller part.

$$\boxed{V_{\text{smaller}}=\dfrac{V}{3\sqrt{3}}=\dfrac{V\sqrt{3}}{9}}$$
